tests.title: In the classroom
tests.transcript: Hello, Mia. Look at the table. The red book is for you. Put the blue pen in the box. Sit next to Tom. The lesson starts now.
items: Where should Mia put the pen?
Who should Mia sit next to?

tests.title: A family photo
tests.transcript: This is my family. My mother is Anna. She has a yellow hat. My father is Ben. He is next to the car. My little sister, Lily, has a small dog.

tests.title: The morning bus
tests.transcript: The number twelve bus leaves at eight fifteen from the station. It stops near Green Street and arrives at the city museum at eight forty. A ticket costs two pounds. Please have your ticket ready.

tests.title: Lucy's weekday
tests.transcript: Lucy gets up at seven every weekday. She eats bread and fruit for breakfast, then walks to school with her brother. Classes finish at three. In the evening, she does her homework before watching television.
items: What does she eat for breakfast?
How does she go to school?
What does she do before television?

tests.title: Changing an appointment
tests.transcript: Hello, this is Northside Dental Clinic calling for Mr Patel. Your appointment on Tuesday at ten thirty must be moved because the dentist is attending a conference. We can offer Wednesday at two or Friday at nine. Please call us before five today to confirm.

tests.title: A weekend market
tests.transcript: The Riverside Market opens this Saturday at nine in the town square. Local farmers will sell fruit, vegetables, cheese, and fresh bread. There will also be music from eleven until one. Visitors should use the free car park behind the sports centre because the square is closed to traffic.
items: How long will the music last?

tests.title: Community garden volunteers
tests.transcript: The community garden is looking for volunteers next Sunday. We will meet at the main gate at half past eight and work until lunchtime. Most people will plant winter vegetables, while a smaller group repairs the wooden fence. Tools are provided, but bring gloves and a bottle of water. If heavy rain is forecast, the event will move to the following weekend.
items: What happens if there is heavy rain?
It moves to the next weekend

tests.title: A delayed rail journey
tests.transcript: Passengers travelling to Brighton should note that the eleven twenty train has been delayed by approximately forty minutes because of a signal failure. You may use your ticket on the eleven forty-five service to Lewes and change there for Brighton. Passengers who decide not to travel can request a full refund from the ticket office.
items: How long is the expected delay?
Who can request a full refund?

tests.title: A revised remote-work policy
tests.transcript: From next month, employees may work remotely for up to three days a week, rather than the current two. Teams must still agree on at least one shared office day to support collaboration. The company will contribute towards home-office equipment, although staff must submit receipts within thirty days. Managers will review the policy after six months, focusing on productivity and employee wellbeing rather than office attendance alone.
items: What is the main policy change?
Why must teams share an office day?
What is required for equipment support?
When will the policy be reviewed?

tests.title: Why cities need small gardens
tests.transcript: Urban planners once treated small community gardens as temporary uses for undeveloped land. Recent research, however, suggests they can reduce local temperatures, absorb rainwater, and strengthen social ties. Their impact depends less on the size of any individual garden than on having a connected network across a neighbourhood. Critics point to maintenance costs, so several cities now fund training rather than relying entirely on unpaid volunteers.
items: How were small gardens previously viewed?

tests.title: Defaults and decision-making
tests.transcript: Behavioural economists have repeatedly shown that default options influence decisions even when changing the default requires little effort. This does not necessarily imply laziness; accepting a default may signal trust in the institution that selected it, or a belief that it reflects a social norm. Consequently, policymakers using defaults must distinguish between helping people act on existing preferences and quietly shaping those preferences. Transparency can reduce manipulation, although overly prominent warnings may also undermine beneficial programmes.
items: What is the speaker's main claim about defaults?
What alternative to laziness is suggested?
What qualification is made about warnings?

tests.title: The limits of energy forecasts
tests.transcript: Forecasts of the energy transition often appear precise because they present a single trajectory for future demand. Yet these projections are conditional stories, not predictions in the strict sense. Small changes in assumptions about storage costs, consumer behaviour, or planning approval can produce sharply different outcomes. Their real value therefore lies in comparing scenarios and exposing trade-offs. Treating one scenario as inevitable can encourage governments to postpone difficult decisions while claiming that technology will resolve them.
items: Why can energy forecasts appear precise?
How does the speaker characterize projections?
What can cause sharply different outcomes?
Where does their real value lie?
What risk follows from treating one scenario as inevitable?

tests.title: Meaning beyond literal language
tests.transcript: Pragmatic competence is sometimes described as the capacity to infer what a speaker intends beyond the literal content of an utterance. That formulation is useful, but deceptively tidy. Intentions are not simply packaged by speakers and retrieved by listeners; they are negotiated against assumptions about status, irony, shared history, and the consequences of being explicit. A listener may recognise several plausible meanings while deliberately leaving the ambiguity unresolved. In such cases, indeterminacy is not a failure of comprehension but a social resource.
items: Why is the common definition called deceptively tidy?
It oversimplifies how intentions are constructed
Status has no effect on language
Which factor is NOT mentioned in interpretation?
What may a skilled listener deliberately do?
Ambiguity can serve a social purpose

tests.title: The ethics of digital archives
tests.transcript: Digitising an archive is often celebrated as an unqualified expansion of access. The claim obscures a tension: materials preserved under conditions of practical obscurity can become instantly searchable, detachable from context, and visible to audiences never imagined by their creators. Restricting access may reproduce institutional gatekeeping, yet unrestricted publication can magnify historical harms. Ethical curation therefore requires more than obtaining legal permission; it demands decisions about description, discoverability, and whether some absences should be respected rather than repaired.
items: What assumption about digitisation is challenged?
What changes when obscure material is digitised?
It becomes searchable and context can detach
It can no longer be restricted
What tension does the speaker identify?
What does respecting some absences imply?
Not every gap should automatically be filled
